deterministicGates.name: Numeric claims carry a source
deterministicGates.detail: 3 paragraph(s) state a figure with no source link and no hedge. The Fact Checker must resolve each.

unresolvedFindings.issue: BLOCKING. The composite note added before the 7:52 a.m. scene - "Maya, Graham, Dev and their company are composites. The pattern is real; the people are not." - asserts a fact about the piece's provenance that no evidence in this run supports, and that the available evidence points against. fact_check.json offers it only as an advisory with TWO options ('add a one-line note that Maya's day is an illustrative composite, or confirm it is true and anonymised'). compliance.json is explicit: 'Yes, it needs a note, and the note must be true. Ask the author to confirm in writing which applies: (a) wholly invented, (b) composite of several people, (c) based on one real workplace... For (c), do not publish until a human decides on identifiability and consent.' No such confirmation exists in the run. Meanwhile the author's own companion draft of the same material (editorial/inbox/most-dangerous-person-b.md) is framed as a real first-person account ('Last spring...', 'Ours was Richard. Eleven years in.', 'She told me later she had drafted the resignation email twice') and closes with HER wording: 'Names and some details have been changed.' seo_geo.json flagged exactly this contradiction: 'the essay is framed as a real account (last spring) while this one reads as a composite. Decide which is true and say so in each.' The integrator rejected the author's own wording on the stated ground that it 'asserts a real event underneath and would create the exposure it is meant to cure' - that is, it selected the lower-liability claim rather than the supported one, which is the opposite of the test compliance set. Asserting 'the people are not [real]' is the one wording that, if wrong, converts an open CL-009 consent question into a published false statement and removes the reader's reason to doubt it. Mitigating and material: the integrator disclosed this in full, twice (changes[0].why: 'CAVEAT FOR THE HUMAN: I cannot verify that the note is true', and forHumanDecision[0]). It is a disclosed defect, not a concealed one.
unresolvedFindings.repair: Do not publish the current wording. Two acceptable fixes, in order of preference. (1) Replace the sentence with wording that is true under every option the author might confirm and that asserts nothing about the people's existence: "Names and identifying details have been changed." That is the author's own Version B wording, it is true under both (b) and (c), and it keeps the note before the scene on both channels as compliance required. (2) If the editor prefers to keep the composite framing, hold the article and obtain the author's written confirmation of (a), (b) or (c) first; on (b) use compliance.json's exact recommended wording, 'Maya, Graham, Dev and the company are composites. Any resemblance to real people is coincidental.'; on (c) do not publish pending a human identifiability and consent decision. Either way, delete the clause 'The pattern is real; the people are not.' - no agent in this run can source it. Keep the existing forHumanDecision entry.

unresolvedFindings.issue: Nineteen words of new narrative action were written into the author's 3:45 p.m. scene: "Dev checks every number in it against the source, because the tool sounds just as certain when it's wrong." Checked against the brief's premise, this was NOT unrecommended: audience.json asks for it under CL-008, and brand_compliance.json suggests 'half a sentence saying a person checked the draft against the data'. CL-008 ('The limit is stated - what it does not do, in the same breath', mandatory, appliesTo all) does plausibly reach this scene, and the docs/02 honesty rule ('Never say a tool is accurate. Say it is often useful and sometimes confidently wrong') supports the phrasing. The rule basis is real, not invented. Two problems remain. First, audience.json made its recommendation conditional - 'State what checking happened, but only if that is what happened in the real account. If it was not checked, the scene should say so' - and the integrator asserted that checking happened with no basis for knowing. Second, brand_compliance.json and editorial.json both assessed CL-008 as ALREADY MET by the existing analysis-section limit ('What it can't do is notice the report nobody opens'), so this is a contested reading of a mandatory rule used to justify inventing a story beat under another writer's byline. Separately, integration.json describes this as 'Added seven words'; it is one 19-word sentence. The quoted text in the same entry is accurate, so this is a counting error in the report, not a concealed edit.
unresolvedFindings.repair: Replace the invented action with a limit statement that asserts no event the author did not write. Delete the clause about Dev and put the limit in narration at the end of that sentence group: "It's ugly. The tool sounds just as certain when it's wrong. It's also four days faster, and short enough that someone might actually read it." That satisfies CL-008 in the same breath, carries the honesty rule, invents nothing, and adds eight words instead of nineteen. Whichever option is chosen, correct the 'seven words' count in integration.json and move the addition into forHumanDecision for author sign-off, because it is narrative content under her byline.

unresolvedFindings.issue: integration.json states 'meaningPreserved: true' and, in meaningNotes, 'Nothing was added that states an opinion on her behalf.' The second claim is false as written. Measured by my own diff: the prose grew from 1425 to 1517 words, of which roughly 85 words are new integrator prose, and three of the additions state positions on the author's behalf - the provenance claim; "A fair question is not overstepping."; and the two closing mechanisms ("Ask her what she noticed, then stand between her and the pressure", "Ask him something neither of you can answer, and admit it first"). Those three are well grounded - audience.json rates both closing gaps HIGH and compliance.json raises the duty-of-care point - and I am not asking for their removal; they are the largest improvement in the piece for the reader it is aimed at. The defect is the self-assessment, not the edit. G6 passes only because it counts first-person tokens: I verified 11 to 11, and that every 'I' and 'me' in the final sits in a line unchanged from the submission, so no invented first person survives. G6 cannot see new third-person prose, and the comment in gates.mjs says the gate exists because 'inventing someone's personal view is the same failure as writing prose under their name'.
unresolvedFindings.repair: Amend integration.json: change meaningNotes to state that about 85 words of new prose were added in the author's third-person voice, list the four insertions (composite note, 3:45 limit sentence, the 'write it down / a fair question is not overstepping' paragraph, the two closing mechanisms), and add them to forHumanDecision as requiring the author's approval before publication. Keep meaningPreserved true only with that amended note attached; the thesis, structure, characters, timeline and conclusions are genuinely untouched.

unresolvedFindings.issue: New unsourced authorial claim in 'The bill': "The quieter version, the invitations that stop arriving, nobody counts at all." This is a universal negative about the state of research, written in the author's voice. It is not in the submission, and nothing in fact_check.json addresses whether workplace exclusion is measured. It does real editorial work - it bridges editorial.json's note that the scene shows exclusion rather than bullying - but it overstates what anyone in this run knows.
unresolvedFindings.repair: Soften to a claim nobody has to source: "The quieter version, the invitations that stop arriving, is harder to count." One shade of emphasis lost, one unsourceable assertion removed.

unresolvedFindings.issue: NON-BLOCKING, ruling requested on brief item 5. The integrator kept both superlatives audience.json flagged - 'the most important thing a manager can do in this decade' and 'One sentence. That's all it takes to stop an immune response' - and disclosed the disagreement openly in rejectedRecommendations. My ruling: the retention is within an editor's authority and the open disclosure is the correct process. docs/02-voice.md principle 3 ('If a sentence needs a superlative to land, it is not true yet') is a real approved-document principle and I cite it as such, but it is not among the 51 rules in policy_snapshot.json, there is no mandatory superlative rule, the author's own approved title is itself a superlative, and editorial.json expressly preserved this passage as the piece's practical lesson. One correction to the record: audience.json cites 'docs/02-voice.md ... Honesty rules: never overclaim' as its source. No such line exists in docs/02; the five honesty rules there concern tool accuracy, vendor endorsement, consent, unsourceable impact numbers, and using someone's story to sell technology. The superlative principle is real; the 'never overclaim' honesty rule is not, and should not be cited as one. Residual substantive point: 'That's all it takes' is an absolute claim that audience.json reasonably says a reader whose manager behaves differently will read as false.
unresolvedFindings.repair: Optional, author's call, not required for publication: delete the four words 'That's all it takes' and keep the paragraph otherwise intact - 'One sentence. Enough to stop an immune response.' Keep 'in this decade' if the author wants it. Record this ruling in integration.json so the disagreement is closed rather than re-raised on a later pass.

unresolvedFindings.issue: Publishing-completeness gap. seo_geo.json produced an seoTitle ('The Most Dangerous Person in the Room Asks Why') and a metaDescription, and the integrator correctly declined to add them to frontmatter the site contract does not ask for - but they now exist only inside a specialist report, and publishing_metadata.json has no field for them. A publisher working from final_article.md plus publishing_metadata.json will never see them. The missing public URL for 'The Great Corporate Unmasking' has the same shape: correctly not invented, correctly flagged, but sitting in a report rather than a handoff. Also recorded: G5 was not run by the integrator, which it disclosed in toolNotes per the brief. I ran it. It reports '1 dead link' for https://workplacebullying.org/2024-wbi-us-survey/ and that is a false positive - I fetched the page myself and it is live, returning 406 to the gate's default user agent. Nobody should treat that G5 result as a defect in the article.
unresolvedFindings.repair: Add the seoTitle and metaDescription to publishing_metadata.json, or to a single handoff block at the top of forHumanDecision, so the LinkedIn and Substack publisher receives them with the article, and keep the Unmasking URL request alongside them. No change to final_article.md is needed for this item.

unresolvedFindings.passage: Maya... Graham... Dev... the VP (whole narrative, 7:52 a.m. to 11:47 p.m.)
unresolvedFindings.explanation: Named characters are presented with no signal that they are invented. The author writes in the first person elsewhere ("I call them Divas", "In The Great Corporate Unmasking, I wrote"), and the scene is a precise, day-long workplace account: fourteen years' tenure, a 2017 failed change, a 2019 wiki page, HR copied on a calendar invite, a predecessor pushed out after eight months. A reader, or a former colleague of the author, can plausibly take this as a real company and real people. Graham is shown acting in bad faith (an HR-copied invite to a newcomer, laughing at her in chat, present when curious people left). If any real person is identifiable, that is defamation and privacy exposure, and there is no consent on file. Nothing in the submission or policy snapshot says the characters are fictional or composite; the author must confirm that. Version B carries 'Names and some details have been changed.' (editorial/inbox/most-dangerous-person-b.md line 129).
unresolvedFindings.recommendation: Yes, it needs a note, and the note must be true. Ask the author to confirm in writing which applies: (a) wholly invented, (b) composite of several people, (c) based on one real workplace. For (a) or (b) use accurate wording such as 'Maya, Graham, Dev and the company are composites. Any resemblance to real people is coincidental.' Do not use 'names have been changed' unless that literally happened, because it asserts a real underlying event. For (c), do not publish until a human decides on identifiability and consent. Put the note before the scene on both LinkedIn and Substack, not only in a footer. Human judgment required; this is not legal clearance.

unresolvedFindings.passage: Nearly half of American adults have been bullied at work or watched it happen, and those targeted face a 62% chance of losing their job.
unresolvedFindings.explanation: Unsourced statistic on a sensitive subject, worded as a probability that a bullied person loses their job. That is a strong claim for readers who may be in that situation. Gate G2 marks it as needing verification. I could not verify it and have not assumed a source. If the figure comes from a survey of reported outcomes, the wording may mislead. It is also US-only in a piece with international readers.
unresolvedFindings.recommendation: Do not publish until the Fact Checker confirms the source, year and exact definition and a link is added. Reword to what the source says, with 'about' where it is an estimate. If unconfirmed, cut the 62% figure.

unresolvedFindings.passage: In MIT Sloan's analysis of employee reviews, toxic culture predicted attrition 10.4 times more strongly than pay. Global engagement fell to 20% in 2025, a loss Gallup puts at about $10 trillion... manager engagement dropped from 27% to 22% in a single year.
unresolvedFindings.explanation: Several third-party research figures attributed to named organisations (MIT Sloan, Gallup) with no links. Misattributing a study to a named institution is an accuracy and reputational risk to both parties. The '10.4 times more strongly' claim is a precise relative-effect figure that is easily misquoted. Flagged by gate G2 and left to the Fact Checker. I have not verified any of them.
unresolvedFindings.recommendation: Each figure needs a primary-source link and a check that the wording matches it. Remove any that cannot be traced.
